title: Exponential advantage in quantum observation with one extra qubit
authors: Zhenyu Du, Xiongfeng Ma, Vlatko Vedral, Jinzhao Sun
problem: Learning how a many-body system evolves often means estimating multi-time correlators, such as the nested commutators that enter nonlinear spectroscopy. Protocols that couple the system to a large quantum memory are known to save exponentially many experiments, but they need about as many extra qubits as the system has. Experiments, however, routinely couple a single controllable probe to the system. Can one extra qubit give an exponential advantage over every protocol that works on the system alone?
result: Yes, in the query model where the unknown evolution \(U\) is applied repeatedly. With one probe qubit, all \(2^k\) nested correlators across \(k+1\) times can be estimated with \(O(Tk/\varepsilon^2)\) applications of \(U\), and the single ordered correlator \(C(U)\) with \(O(T/\varepsilon^2)\). Any protocol confined to the \(n\)-qubit system, even with unlimited coherence time and adaptive mid-circuit operations, needs \(\Omega(k2^k)\) and \(\Omega(2^k)\) applications respectively when \(T=k\le n/5\). Protocols that cannot keep coherence across \(k\) applications need \(2^{\Omega(n)}\), whatever their memory.
significance: The separation needs the smallest possible quantum memory, one qubit, and holds against a much stronger baseline than earlier memory-advantage results. The resource is interference between two dynamical histories, which a single probe can create and a system-only protocol cannot. The protocol uses non-adaptive probe–system interactions available in current simulators and sensors, and the coherence-time result says that memory time, not only memory size, is a source of exponential advantage.
limitations: The lower bounds hold for a constructed family of hard evolutions that hides the signal behind Haar-random bases; they do not show that the advantage holds for every physical Hamiltonian, and the numerical example (ten spins, mixed-field Ising chain) shows a factor of about 100 in runs rather than an exponential. Observables are taken to be unitary, the system-only model forbids any extra memory, and the counted resource is applications of \(U\), not wall-clock time. The lower-bound proofs occupy long appendices that were not read here.

methods_source_section: Sec. II.1 (Eqs. (1)–(3), Theorem 1, Fig. 2); Sec. II.2 (Eq. (4), Theorem 2); Sec. II.3 (Theorem 3)
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The task is to characterize an unknown evolution \(U\) of \(n\) qubits by estimating correlators of observables \(O_1,\dots,O_{k+1}\) at times \(t_1\le\dots\le t_{k+1}=T\). Each binary string \(\sigma\) picks commutators or anticommutators at each nesting level, giving a family of \(2^k\) real correlators \(F_\sigma(U)\); the ordered correlator \(C(U)=\mathrm{Tr}[O_{k+1}(t_{k+1})\cdots O_1(t_1)\rho]\) is another target. Cost is counted as the total number of applications of \(U\) over all runs.

Two machines are compared. A system-only machine applies \(U\) to the \(n\)-qubit register and may do anything in between, adaptively and with unlimited coherence time, but keeps no quantum memory beyond the system. A probe machine adds one qubit that stays coherent between applications of \(U\), interacts with the system in a fixed pattern, and is measured with the system at the end.

The probe algorithm rests on an identity: every nested correlator is a Walsh–Hadamard transform of overlaps between pairs of complementary histories, in which each observable is inserted on exactly one of the two branches. The overlaps do not depend on \(\sigma\), so one randomized experiment estimates all of them, much as classical shadows estimate many observables from one set of snapshots. Choosing the all-ones history recovers a known single-probe interferometric scheme for \(C(U)\).

The lower bounds use a family of evolutions in which the signal sits in a relative phase between two long histories whose intermediate states are scrambled by Haar-random bases. A probe can interfere the two histories directly. A system-only protocol must navigate the random bases blind, and the authors show that the coherence it can maintain between the histories, and hence what it learns about the hidden phase, shrinks exponentially with \(k\). A simulation with \(2^{24}\) runs on a ten-spin chain recovers all 256 correlators with about ten times lower error than estimating each separately with the same budget.

methods.technique: Nested correlators as a Walsh–Hadamard transform of complementary-path overlaps
methods.explanation: Expanding each commutator or anticommutator produces terms in which each observable acts either before or after the others in the trace. Grouping terms by which observables sit on the ket side and which on the bra side gives overlaps between two histories, and the signs from the commutators form a Walsh–Hadamard character.
math: For a string \(b\in\{0,1\}^k\) define the history and the complementary overlap \[W_b=U^{t_{k+1}-t_k}O_k^{b_k}\cdots U^{t_2-t_1}O_1^{b_1}U^{t_1},\qquad Q_b=\mathrm{Tr}\bigl(O_{k+1}W_b\rho W_{\bar b}^\dagger\bigr),\] where \(\bar b=1-b\). The paper's identity is \(F_\sigma(U)=\frac{i^{|\sigma|}}{2}\,\mathbb E_b\bigl[(-1)^{\sigma\cdot b}Q_b\bigr]\).

Editorial check for \(k=1\). Here \(Q_1=\mathrm{Tr}[\rho\,O_2(t_2)O_1(t_1)]\) and \(Q_0=\mathrm{Tr}[\rho\,O_1(t_1)O_2(t_2)]\). The anticommutator correlator is \(F_0=\tfrac14\mathrm{Tr}[\rho\{O_2(t_2),O_1(t_1)\}]=\tfrac14(Q_0+Q_1)\), and the commutator correlator is \[F_1=\frac{-i}{4}\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[\rho\,[O_2(t_2),O_1(t_1)]\bigr]=\frac{i}{4}(Q_0-Q_1),\] both matching the identity. Editorial numerical check: for a random three-qubit unitary, random Pauli observables and \(k=3\), the identity agrees with the direct formula to \(10^{-16}\) for all eight \(\sigma\).

Since \(|Q_b|\le1\), an unbiased estimate of each \(Q_b\) with bounded variance, for \(b\) drawn uniformly, gives an unbiased estimate of every \(F_\sigma\) from the same data. Hoeffding's inequality with a union bound over \(2^k\) targets needs \(O(\log(2^k)/\varepsilon^2)=O(k/\varepsilon^2)\) runs, each using \(T\) applications of \(U\), which is the \(O(Tk/\varepsilon^2)\) of Theorem 1.
methods.transfer: When many target quantities are different signed combinations of the same underlying overlaps, sampling the overlaps once and applying the transform afterwards replaces a separate experiment per target. The same structure appears in nonlinear response functions and in Pauli-weight decompositions.

methods.technique: Interfering two histories with one probe qubit
methods.explanation: A probe in \(\ket+\) controls which branch receives each observable. At the end the two branches have evolved along histories \(W_b\) and \(W_{\bar b}\), and measuring the probe in the \(X\) or \(Y\) basis together with \(O_{k+1}\) reads out their overlap, which no single history reveals.
math: Editorial derivation. Start from \(\ket+\otimes\ket\psi\). At step \(j\) apply \(O_j\) to the system on the probe-\(1\) branch if \(b_j=1\), and on the probe-\(0\) branch otherwise, with \(U\) applied in between to both branches. The final state is \(\frac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0\ket{\psi_{\bar b}}+\ket1\ket{\psi_b}\bigr)\) with \(\ket{\psi_b}=W_b\ket\psi\). For Hermitian \(O=O_{k+1}\), \[\langle X\otimes O\rangle=\mathrm{Re}\,\langle\psi_{\bar b}|O|\psi_b\rangle,\qquad\langle Y\otimes O\rangle=\mathrm{Im}\,\langle\psi_{\bar b}|O|\psi_b\rangle,\] and \(\langle\psi_{\bar b}|O|\psi_b\rangle=Q_b\).

A system-only machine never holds the two histories in superposition: every quantity it measures is an expectation value in one evolving state. In the hard family the hidden phase between the two histories is the signal. The paper reduces any system-only protocol to a simplified ideal process and proves there that the coherence between the two paths contracts as the protocol works through the scrambled steps, so its measurement records for the two values of the phase stay nearly indistinguishable unless it uses \(\Omega(2^k)\) applications of \(U\).

The coherence-time theorem follows the same picture: a protocol must keep coherence across all \(k\) applications of \(U\) to interfere the two full histories. With at most \(L<k\) applications per run, even unbounded memory needs \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) applications, so the probe protocol, which uses exactly \(k\) applications per run for consecutive times, is optimal in both memory size and memory time.
methods.transfer: A single control qubit that routes operator insertions between two branches turns hidden relative phases into measurable expectation values. The construction is the basis of echo and out-of-time-order measurements and can be reused wherever a signal is encoded in the interference of two histories.
